examples.ko: 갑작스레 비가 내려서 우산이 없어 곤란했어요.
examples.en: It suddenly rained and I had no umbrella, so I was in trouble.
A friend dropped by unexpectedly and I was surprised.
The company suddenly told me to go on a business trip.

examples.ko: 그는 이야기를 하다가 갑작스레 눈물을 흘렸어요.
examples.en: While talking, he suddenly shed tears.

examples.ko: 날씨가 갑작스레 추워져서 옷을 더 입었어요.
examples.en: The weather turned cold suddenly, so I put on more clothes.

examples.ko: 갑작스레 불이 꺼져서 모두 소리를 질렀어요.
examples.en: The lights went out suddenly and everyone screamed.

explain: 갑작스레는 '갑자기'보다 조금 글 같고 부드러운 느낌이에요. 대화에서는 '갑자기'를 훨씬 많이 쓰고, 뉴스에서는 '갑작스러운 사고'처럼 '갑작스럽다'도 자주 써요. 꾸미는 말이라 '갑작스레 말하다'처럼 동사 앞에 놓아요.
explain_en: 갑작스레 feels a bit more written and soft than 갑자기. In speech 갑자기 is far more common, and the news often uses the adjective form, as in 갑작스러운 사고. It is an adverb and sits before the verb, as in 갑작스레 말하다.

examples.ko: 우리 다 같이 건배해요! 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
examples.en: Let's all raise our glasses! Happy New Year.

examples.ko: 건배 소리가 식당 안에 크게 울렸어요.
examples.en: The sound of the toast rang out loudly in the restaurant.
The teacher proposed a toast.
We toasted with juice and ate cake.
We wrapped up the gathering with a toast at the end.
When you toast, you clink the glasses lightly.

explain: 한국에서는 '건배!'라고 외치며 잔을 부딪치는 것이 모임의 시작이나 끝 인사 같아요. 술이 아니라 음료수로 해도 괜찮아요. '위하여!'는 누군가를 위해 건배할 때 같이 외쳐요.
explain_en: In Korea, shouting 건배! and clinking glasses is like a greeting at the start or end of a gathering. You can do it with soft drinks too. People also shout 위하여! when toasting to someone or something.

en: to be exaggerated; to be overstated

examples.en: The rumor is blown way out of proportion.
I think the news is exaggerated.
The story got more exaggerated as it was passed on.
What you see in the ad is overstated.
Did what I said sound exaggerated?
That story might be exaggerated.

explain: '과장되다'는 이야기나 표현이 실제보다 커졌다고 볼 때 써요. 말하는 사람이 일부러 그러면 '과장하다'예요. 소문, 광고, 표현, 연기 같은 말과 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: 과장되다 describes a story or expression that has become bigger than reality. If the speaker does it on purpose, use 과장하다. It fits well with rumors, ads, expressions and acting.

examples.ko: 다음 달부터 택시 기본요금이 또 올라요.
examples.en: From next month, the basic taxi fare goes up again.

examples.ko: 기본요금만 내면 오 킬로미터까지 갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you only pay the basic fare, you can go up to five kilometers.
Data is included in the phone's basic charge.
The distance was short, so it came to only the basic fare.
I first asked how much the basic charge was.

examples.ko: 기본요금 이후에는 거리에 따라 요금이 더 붙어요.
examples.en: After the basic charge, more is added depending on distance.

explain: 택시, 휴대폰, 주차장처럼 처음에 내야 하는 최소 요금을 말해요. 그 뒤에 이용한 만큼 더 내는 것은 '추가 요금'이라고 해요. '기본료'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: It is the minimum fee you pay at the start for things like taxis, phone plans and parking. What you pay on top of that, depending on use, is called '추가 요금'. People also say '기본료'.

en: to become dull; to flag; to droop

examples.en: I prepared everything and now it's canceled, what a letdown.
You told me the ending first, so it ruined the fun.
Why spoil it by telling me in advance?

examples.ko: 기대했던 경기가 일찍 끝나서 김샌 기분이에요.
examples.en: The game I was looking forward to ended early, so I feel let down.

examples.ko: 이제 와서 안 가겠다고 하면 김새잖아요.
examples.en: If you say you won't go now, it kills the mood.

examples.ko: 김새지 않게 계획은 비밀로 해 주세요.
examples.en: Please keep the plan secret so it doesn't spoil the fun.

explain: '김이 새다'가 줄어든 구어체 표현이고, 기대하거나 신나던 마음이 갑자기 꺾일 때 써요. 친한 사이에서 편하게 하는 말이라 윗사람에게는 조심해서 써요.
explain_en: It is a contracted spoken form of '김이 새다' and is used when excitement or anticipation suddenly gets deflated. It is casual talk between close people, so be careful using it with superiors.

examples.en: I can hear a siren far away.
An ambulance passed by with its siren going.
When the siren sounded, the cars made way.
A siren in the middle of the night startled me awake.
The police car arrived quietly without a siren.
A siren quickly grabs people's attention.

explain: 구급차, 소방차, 경찰차에서 나는 소리와 그 장치를 모두 가리켜요. 소리가 날 때는 '사이렌이 울리다', 소리를 내게 할 때는 '사이렌을 울리다'라고 말해요.
explain_en: It means both the sound made by ambulances, fire trucks and police cars and the device itself. When it sounds, say '사이렌이 울리다'; when someone sets it off, '사이렌을 울리다'.

examples.ko: 올림픽 대표 선발전이 다음 달에 열려요.
examples.en: The Olympic team trials will be held next month.

examples.ko: 선발전에서 1등을 해야 국가대표가 될 수 있어요.
examples.en: You have to finish first in the trials to become a national team member.
My younger sibling practices every day to prepare for the trials.

examples.ko: 이번 선발전에는 백 명이 넘게 참가했어요.
examples.en: More than a hundred people took part in these trials.
I heard the results of the trials will be announced tomorrow.
Sadly, I couldn't make it past the trials.

explain: '시험'이나 '오디션'이 사람을 평가하는 일이라면, 선발전은 경기를 해서 이긴 사람이 뽑히는 방식이에요. 주로 '국가대표 선발전'처럼 스포츠에서 써요. 노래나 연기는 '오디션', 일반 회사는 '채용'이라고 구별해요.
explain_en: While '시험' and '오디션' evaluate people, a 선발전 picks winners by having them compete. It is mainly used in sports, as in '국가대표 선발전'. For singing or acting you say '오디션', and for ordinary companies '채용'.

examples.en: I was shocked by the sudden news.
I could not speak for a while because of the shock.
That accident was a shock to everyone.

examples.ko: 쇼크가 너무 커서 잠이 안 와요.
examples.en: The shock is so big that I cannot sleep.
He was taken to the hospital in a state of shock.
It takes time to get over the shock.

explain: 마음의 충격은 '충격'과 비슷하게 '쇼크를 받다', '충격을 받다'라고 해요. '쇼크 상태'는 몸에 생기는 의학 용어로도 써요.
explain_en: For mental impact, 'shock' works much like 'chunggyeok': 'syokeureul batda' and 'chunggyeogeul batda'. 'Syokeu sangtae' is also a medical term for a physical state.

examples.ko: 쌀통 바닥에 쌀알이 조금 남아 있어요.
examples.en: A few grains of rice are left at the bottom of the rice bin.
The rice grains are plump, so the rice tastes good.
Each grain of this rice is long and slender.
Rice grains have fallen on the kitchen floor.
Birds peck at the rice grains in the yard.
When you cook porridge, the rice grains gradually swell.

explain: 익히지 않은 쌀의 낱알은 '쌀알', 지은 밥의 낱알은 '밥알'이라고 구분해요. 그래서 밥 먹다가 말할 때는 보통 '밥알'을 써요. 소리 나는 대로 [싸랄]이라고 읽어요.
explain_en: A single uncooked grain is a '쌀알', while a grain of cooked rice is a '밥알'. So when talking about eating a meal, people usually say '밥알'. It is pronounced [싸랄].

examples.en: An employee leaked company secrets outside.

examples.ko: 공장에서 기름을 바다에 유출한 사고가 있었어요.
examples.en: There was an accident where a factory spilled oil into the sea.

examples.ko: 개인 정보를 유출하면 큰 문제가 돼요.
examples.en: Leaking personal information becomes a serious problem.
He was punished for leaking the exam questions.
I changed the password so the data wouldn't leak.

examples.ko: 사진을 유출한 사람을 아직 못 찾았어요.
examples.en: They still haven't found the person who leaked the photo.

explain: 정보나 물질이 안에서 밖으로 새어 나가게 하는 것이에요. 사람이 주어이면 '유출하다', 정보나 기름이 주어이면 '유출되다'를 써요. 뉴스에서 정보, 기술, 기름 이야기에 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It means letting information or substances leak from inside to outside. With a person as the subject use 유출하다; with the information or oil as the subject use 유출되다. It often appears in news about data, technology, and oil.

examples.en: The children jump around excitedly.
The player jumped high and caught the ball.

examples.ko: 강 건너로 점프할 수 있을 것 같아요?
examples.en: Do you think you can jump across the stream?
Bend your knees before you jump.
The cat jumped lightly onto the chair.
I took a photo of the jumping motion.

explain: 영어 jump에서 온 외래어예요. 운동, 게임, 놀이처럼 몸을 높이 뛰어오를 때 자주 써요. 일상 한국어에서는 '뛰다', '뛰어오르다'도 많이 쓰고, 한 단계를 건너뛰는 건 '건너뛰다'라고 해요.
explain_en: This is a loanword from English jump, common in sports, games, and play when someone leaps up. Everyday Korean also uses 뛰다 and 뛰어오르다, and skipping a step is 건너뛰다.

examples.en: When making kimchi, we add salted shrimp.
A plate of salted seafood was set on the table.
Jeot is salty, so I only eat a little.
They sell many kinds of salted seafood at the market.
Grandmother makes her own salted seafood.

examples.ko: 오래 삭힌 젓이 더 깊은 맛이 나요.
examples.en: Seafood fermented for a long time has a deeper flavor.

explain: '젓'은 새우, 멸치, 조개 같은 해산물을 소금에 절여 삭힌 음식이에요. '새우젓', '멸치젓', '명란젓'처럼 재료 이름 뒤에 붙여 써요. 김치를 담글 때 감칠맛을 더하는 양념으로도 자주 쓰여요. 발음은 [젇]이에요.
explain_en: 젓 is seafood such as shrimp, anchovy or shellfish that has been salted and fermented. It attaches to the ingredient name, as in 새우젓, 멸치젓 and 명란젓. It is also often used as a seasoning to add savory depth to kimchi. It is pronounced [젇].

examples.ko: 이번 달 지출액이 지난달보다 많이 늘었어요.
examples.en: This month's spending went up a lot compared to last month.

examples.ko: 가계부를 쓰면 한 달 지출액을 한눈에 볼 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you keep a household ledger, you can see a month's spending at a glance.

examples.ko: 지출액 중에서 식비가 가장 큰 부분을 차지해요.
examples.en: Of all my expenses, food takes up the biggest part.
I'm cutting back on eating out to reduce my spending.
My salary stays the same, but only my expenses keep growing.

examples.ko: 지출액과 수입액을 비교해서 표로 만들어 봤어요.
examples.en: I compared my expenses and income and made a table.

explain: '수입액'과 짝으로 써서 번 돈과 쓴 돈을 비교할 때 많이 나와요. 일상 대화에서는 '쓴 돈', '나간 돈'이라고도 말해요. '늘다/줄다', '많다/적다'와 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: It pairs with '수입액' (income) when comparing money earned and money spent. In everyday talk people also say '쓴 돈' or '나간 돈'. It goes well with '늘다/줄다' and '많다/적다'.
